First Owner Got No-Markup Plymouth Superbird, Picked It Up After 6 Months, It's an Amazing Survivor
31 photos
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150
Rain-soaked timber country rarely advertises its greatest mechanical treasures, and the quiet logging town of Vernonia, Oregon is no exception. Behind the weathered brick facade of the former Vernonia Auto Company—a historic dealership that first opened its doors to sell new 1938 Chevrolets—restorer and lifelong collector Gary Myers presides over a subterranean labyrinth of Detroit iron that will leave you speechless.
Stepping past an original 1938 porcelain neon dealership sign is like crossing the threshold into an untouched muscle car sanctuary. Parked nose-to-tail across two crowded levels sit two 1970 Plymouth Superbirds, a 19,000-mile (30,578-kilometer) 1969 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner coupe, a 1-of-36 1968 Plymouth Hemi GTX convertible, a California black-plate 1968 Dodge Hemi Charger, and a genuine 1970 Plymouth Road Runner 440 Six-Barrel bought for a single $100 bill.
The roster stretches even further into the shadows of the workshop. A Spring Green 1969 Dodge Charger R/T reunited with its factory drivetrain shares floor space with a triple-color 1969 Road Runner convertible, a heavily documented 1970 Road Runner 383 in Limelight green, an unrestored 1971 Chevrolet Camaro Z28 bearing a 1970s bullet hole, a 1962 Chevrolet Impala, a record-breaking Road Runner circle-track racer, and a dozen customer Mopars.
Yet every visitor's gaze inevitably locks onto the brightest jewel parked on the upper floor beside that glowing powder-blue Chevrolet neon sign. It is Gary's unrestored, 40,000-mile (64,374-kilometer) 1970 Plymouth Road Runner Superbird, a factory pistol-grip 4-speed survivor that wears its original paint, original vinyl top, and original factory assembly scars like badges of honor from the fiercest aerodynamic war in American stock car racing history.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 To comprehend why such an outrageous machine ever rolled onto public streets, one must revisit the high-banked superspeedways of 1969. Chrysler Corporation was locked in a 200-mph aerodynamic battle against Ford Motor Company, and was losing. The Torino Talladega was mopping the floors with Mopar rivals, while then-triple champion Richard Petty had defected to Ford after Plymouth executives refused to build him a winged counterpart to the 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona.
Determined to win Petty back for 1970 – and the NASCAR wreath of laurels – Plymouth went to work, calling the missile engineers back for another round of wind-tunnel wizardry. While Dodge had satisfied 1969 racing rules by building just 503 Charger Daytonas—reportedly tricking inspectors by driving the same cars past counting officials twice—sanctioning officials raised the 1970 homologation mandate to one vehicle for every two franchised dealerships in the United States.
Offered for just a single model year in 1970, the Superbird required a minimum run of 1,920 cars, with Plymouth ultimately assembling a few extras, just to be on the safe side in case someone actually wanted to count each and every one of those. The most commonly accepted version is that there are 1,935 units, all assembled in late 1969. Quite a few are accounted for today - several of those have been rescued by Troy Bergeron, Mopars5150’s head car nut, who came to visit Gary and his collection.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Buyers in 1970 could select from three big-block engines: the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8 rated at 425 hp (431 PS) and 490 lb-ft (664 Nm) of torque with 135 built, the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Six-Barrel V8 making 390 hp (395 PS) with 716 built, or the standard 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Super Commando 4-barrel V8 producing 375 hp (380 PS) and 480 lb-ft (651 Nm) with 1,084 built, of which 4-speed manuals were 485.
Gary's 4-speed survivor hails from the third and final production batch, where workers at Detroit's Lynch Road plant and Clairpointe facility slammed the cars together to beat the December 31, 1969 deadline. As Gary demonstrates, the Superbird is literally a corporate half-breed: engineers grafted the 19-inch steel nose cone onto a Plymouth Road Runner body by bolting on modified front fenders and the hood from a 1970 Dodge Coronet.
Because this car has never been restored, every chaotic detail of that rushed 1969 assembly line remains preserved. Pitted air pockets and coarse grinder marks mar the factory lead filler around the nose cone, stray welding wires protrude from the hinges, factory paint runs drip down the door jambs, and inspector grease-pencil numerals—a 7 on one side and a 6 on the other—still grace the Dana 60 rear axle.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Despite its speedway pedigree, the towering 24-inch (610-millimeter) cast-aluminum rear wing repelled suburban buyers in 1970. A physician bought this car new at dealer cost on the condition that it remain on the showroom floor for six months to draw curious traffic. When he finally brought it home, his wife refused to ride in it unless the wing was removed, leaving minor scratches around the trunk mounting cutouts.
The doctor's son later drove the Superbird to college, clamping a ski rack directly onto the black vinyl roof pillars to haul snow skis up to Oregon mountain lodges. In June 1999, a friend sent Gary to Lowell, Oregon to inspect the car as a practical joke; the prank backfired when Gary bought the time capsule and later verified those exact ski-rack rub marks in a stunned phone call with the original owner's son.
Today, the car retains three original paper broadcast sheets—including one still tucked untouched beneath the center floor mat—alongside its original window sticker and ink-stamped spare tire. While Gary and his wife once drove it down Interstate 5 to Woodburn, dodging distracted motorists and 40-foot (12.2-meter) semi-trucks, this irreplicable piece of racing history now rests safely indoors, never to be sold during Gary's lifetime.
